title: Same demand rise, different supply

readouts.v: P2/P1 = 1.2^(1/(PES + 0.5)) (D has PED 0.5 in absolute value)

predict.q: Demand rises (D1 → D2). Supply is very inelastic (PES = 0.25). What happens?

options.s: Price rises a lot; quantity rises a little
options.fb: With PES 0.25 firms can hardly expand output, so the price does the adjusting: price +27.5%, quantity +6.3%.

options.s: Quantity rises a lot; price rises a little
options.fb: That happens when supply is elastic. Move the slider up to 3 to see it.

options.s: Price and quantity rise by the same percentage
options.fb: Equal percentage changes happen only at PES = 1.

options.s: Nothing happens, because supply has not shifted
options.fb: Supply did not shift, but demand did. The market moves along the supply curve: an extension of supply.

task: Switch demand to **D2**. Then move the **PES** slider from 0.25 up to 3 and watch the new equilibrium. Then set PES = 0.

target.do: Switch demand to D2 (keep PES at 0.25), then press Check.

takeaway: The less elastic supply is, the more a rise in demand shows up as a **higher price** rather than more output.
explore: Try PES 1 (both +12.9%), PES 3 (price +5.3%, quantity +16.9%) and PES 0 (price +44%, quantity 0).
